shipping.title: Shipping policy
body: We ship worldwide. Orders leave within 24–48 hours. Delivery is typically 4–7 business days depending on location.
Orders over €150 include free worldwide shipping. Below that, shipping is calculated at checkout.
After dispatch you receive a track-and-trace code. Please enter your address correctly — we cannot take responsibility for packages lost to an incorrect address.

refund.title: Returns & refunds
body: You have 14 days from the date of receipt to return items without giving a reason. The return must be sent within those 14 days.
Items must be unworn, unwashed and in original packaging with the hangtag uncut. Wear, stains, holes or scent will be refused.
Once we receive the return, refunds are issued within 10 working days, then up to 3 days to appear on your statement. Exchanges follow the same return flow.

about.lede: The faces behind Anovair; we are Tim and Maurice, childhood friends and founders of the brand.
body: Both having a strong desire for past times we never even have experienced ourselves, this sense of nostalgia is the heartbeat of Anovair.

Driven by our obsession with vintage styles, we created Anovair; a platform for reinventing the past. The past has something magical, and we seek to revive it through our platform. Combining our passion for vintage fashion, music, and culture.
We hope to reach and connect like-minded individuals, bringing back the ‘good old days’.

journal.title: Matthew McConaughey: The Anti-Fashion Formula
journal.author: Raul Ferrer
journal.excerpt: Uvalde, Texas, 1969. Austin, 1993. Hollywood, ever since. The story of Matthew McConaughey — the anti-fashion man who quietly became one of the most copied dressers in American style.
journal.dek: On the Texas boy who taught Hollywood that character always beats styling.
body: Matthew McConaughey’s style is defined by three constants: worn-in essentials — white T-shirts, faded denim, suede jackets — a subtle Southern influence rooted in Texas ranch and western dressing, and a complete refusal of trend-driven fashion.

Hollywood’s least-dressed man is also its most copied. For over thirty years, effortless style has never been about trends. It has been about wearing timeless pieces until they become unmistakably yours.
Matthew David McConaughey was born on 4 November 1969 in Uvalde, Texas. Texas was the constant — its landscape, its dress code, its refusal to be impressed by outside standards.

In 1992 he auditioned for Richard Linklater’s Dazed and Confused. The role was David Wooderson. He was on screen for less than ten minutes. The look — tight jeans, white T-shirt, unbuttoned shirt, boots — became instantly recognisable. He had, at twenty-three, walked into his uniform. He never left it.
The McConaissance years added intention without abandoning Wooderson: a heavier white tee, cleaner denim, suede and worn leather. The wardrobe of a man who had decided, on his own terms, who he was.
Six pieces do most of the work: a heavyweight white T-shirt, faded straight-leg denim, a tan suede jacket, a worn brown leather jacket, a white cotton dress shirt, and broken-in leather boots.
Buy fewer pieces and wear them harder. Trust neutrals. One Western element, never more. Never look like you are trying. Age the wardrobe on purpose.

journal.title: Pinstripe Shirt: History, Style & How to Wear It (2026 Guide)
journal.author: Raul Ferrer
journal.excerpt: From Jermyn Street in 1910 to a villa outside Saint-Tropez in 1969 — the complete guide to the pinstripe shirt, its Italian collar, and how to wear it correctly today.

journal.title: Jude Law Style: The Art of Understatement
journal.author: Raul Ferrer
journal.excerpt: From Dickie Greenleaf in Mongibello to Notting Hill on a Sunday morning — the story of Jude Law, and the wardrobe of restraint that made him one of the most quietly influential men in menswear.
body: Jude Law’s influence on menswear is quiet on purpose. The camera found him in The Talented Mr. Ripley as Dickie Greenleaf — linen, open collars, a suntan, and the kind of ease that cannot be shopped in a weekend.
Understatement is the whole point. Soft tailoring instead of sharp. Neutrals instead of statements. A shirt that looks lived-in rather than pressed for a lookbook.
The modern reading of Law is Sunday in Notting Hill: a knit, a trouser with a crease that isn’t trying, loafers or a simple sneaker. Nothing branded. Everything considered.
That is the Anovair register too — pieces that belong to a life, not a season.

journal.title: Diego Maradona: The King of Naples
journal.author: Raul Ferrer
journal.excerpt: Villa Fiorito, 1960. Naples, 1984. The story of Diego Maradona — the boy from a Buenos Aires slum who arrived in Naples with nothing and made a city his throne for seven years.

journal.title: David Beckham: The Last English Gentleman
journal.author: Raul Ferrer
journal.excerpt: Leytonstone, 1975. The Cotswolds, 2026. The story of David Beckham — the footballer who became the last English gentleman, and built a wardrobe to match.

journal.title: Frank Sinatra: The Chairman of the Board
journal.author: Raul Ferrer
journal.excerpt: Hoboken, 1915. The Sands, 1960. The world Frank Sinatra moved through is gone — what remains is the wardrobe, and the standard it set.

journal.title: Richard Gere: The Style of a New Kind of Man
journal.author: Raul Ferrer
journal.excerpt: In 1980, a thirty-year-old actor laid out a row of Armani shirts on a Los Angeles bed, and menswear was never the same.

journal.title: Manhattan: The Style of a Decade
journal.author: Raul Ferrer
journal.excerpt: Manhattan, the 1990s. Calvin Klein on Madison Avenue, Helmut Lang on Greene Street. The story of the pleated trouser — born in 1920s England, perfected in 1990s New York.

journal.title: Carolyn Bessette Style: 90s Minimalism Returns
journal.author: Raul Ferrer
journal.excerpt: Manhattan, 1996. A dark indigo straight-leg jean, a white tee, a camel coat. The story of Carolyn Bessette and the 1990s minimalism she defined.

journal.title: The Breton Striped Shirt: A History of the Marinière
journal.author: Raul Ferrer
journal.excerpt: The Breton striped shirt — la marinière — was officially adopted by the French Navy in 1858, with 21 stripes representing Napoleon’s naval victories.

journal.title: La Piscine: The Style of a Riviera Summer
journal.author: Raul Ferrer
journal.excerpt: Saint-Tropez, 1969. A villa, a pool, two former lovers, and a pale blue pinstripe shirt. How Alain Delon taught the world how to wear a shirt.

journal.title: The Henley Shirt: A History of the Modern Classic
journal.author: Raul Ferrer
journal.excerpt: The Henley shirt began on a stretch of the Thames in 1839 — designed for rowers, adopted by labourers, immortalised by Hollywood.
journal.dek: From the rivers of England to the heart of the modern wardrobe.
body: The Henley shirt has lived several lives. It began as workwear for rowers on a stretch of the Thames. It became a uniform for labourers, then military issue, then a Hollywood favourite.
Not every moment calls for a T-shirt, and not every moment calls for a polo. The Henley fills the space between — knit fabric for comfort, a placket for structure.

It takes its name from Henley-on-Thames. The Royal Regatta, founded in 1839, dressed rowers in a pullover with a buttoned placket so the shirt could be pulled over the head and the neck could move with every stroke. By the late 19th century the name had stuck.

Steve McQueen wore Henleys on and off set throughout the 1960s and 1970s — often in cream, often pushed up the forearms, always with the buttons undone. Paul Newman wore them. Robert Redford wore them.
Wear it close to the body. Leave the top button undone. Layer it under a Harrington, suede or wool. Keep to black, white, grey, navy and earth — loud colours fight the garment’s nature.
The men at Henley-on-Thames did not know they were inventing anything. The best garments tend to be born that way.
